Homeless Wichitans near Chapin Park left in the dark on their future

As the city’s undetermined closing date for the encampment looms, those who live there are exasperated at what they say is a lack of communication.
by Stefania Lugli August 21, 2026August 21, 2026

Share this:

  • Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook
  • Share on X (Opens in new window) X
  • Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email

Residents of Wichita’s largest homeless encampment are frustrated.

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 7:30
Instaread

After years of living cloistered from the public in woods just north of Chapin Park, more than 80 people soon will be evicted by the city from an encampment that’s come to be home for them. 

Chapin’s residents told The Journal this month that they are stressed and angry over what they perceive as bureaucratic disorganization and a lack of communication. Regardless of the outside world’s opinion of their lifestyles, their encampment is a community that’s currently subject solely to the will of local government.

City officials recently confirmed to The Journal plans to raze the encampment, saying that an increase in activity is making people feel unsafe. The site, at risk of flooding due to its proximity to the river, also isn’t considered suitable for human habitation.

Bobby Redgate and his partner, Shannon, have lived at the site for over three years. Redgate said that there have been visits from case managers, but he wasn’t sure if they were from city housing, United Way of the Plains or another nonprofit.

“Them going out regularly and letting us know what’s going on and what their plans are? Nonexistent. How are we supposed to know what’s going on if we’re left in the dark? If I get moved into a place, I got more than a month’s worth of moving to do,” he said. “I need to know this ASAP.

“And today, this is August, and they’re talking about throwing people out and doing this and that. Some of us ain’t even got nowhere yet.” Redgate said he last saw a case manager a few weeks ago, who needed copies of Shannon’s Social Security card and ID for processing.

Residents interviewed at the encampment don’t have a shared view on what the future of their site is. Some have heard that the closure has been put on pause, maybe indefinitely. Others cite a late August closing date. A few said they think the camp is closing, but that there was a holdup due to some ambiguity regarding the ownership of the land they live on. (The Kansas Department of Transportation owns it and is collaborating with the city on the camp’s cleanup.)

In their effort to figure out what to expect, several residents sought information from this reporter about the site’s uncertain future. The city, as of Aug. 20, says there is still no closing date. 

There is confusion, too, over what housing vouchers, if any, are available for them. Almost every person has a different understanding of the timeline. Conflicting rumors over the availability of  vouchers and case managers are rampant. 

When asked, the city said that there are enough case managers for those already engaged with housing and there is no waitlist for vouchers. 

“Navigating someone through the process is labor intensive and takes time,” said Tyler Schiffelbein, a spokesperson for the city. 

Where there is a staff shortage? Assisting with move-ins and post move-in check-ins. The post-housing phase is crucial, especially for those who have been chronically homeless and may have not lived in an apartment for years. It is common for people to return to homelessness because of a lack of wraparound services or peer support.

The right to due process

Michelle Ewert, a professor at Washburn University’s School of Law and director of the Washburn Law Clinic, recently visited the Chapin encampment and spoke with several residents. 

“It’s concerning that there is such confusion among the encampment residents about what is happening. That shows that they have not received clear communication about what the next steps are,” she said.

Ewert, who has represented other homeless people in court, said that they have the right to due process, even in locations with illegal-camping ordinances, like Wichita.

“The government has to provide due process if they’re going to deprive someone of property,” she said. “And courts have found that in the context of encampment clearing, residents are entitled to advance notice before the eviction occurs.”

This can be done through posted flyers or conversations with government workers, but whatever form the notice takes should be clear and consistent. In addition, she said, due process can require state or local government to store belongings for a period of time after an encampment is cleared out.

Ewert pointed to a 2012 case out of Los Angeles, in which the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that unabandoned legal papers, shelter and other effects are personal property that cannot be taken and destroyed without providing notice to the owners and offering a chance for reclamation.

‘Good people’ with nowhere to go

Chapin is a tightly knit community. There have been issues of crime and fires, but for the most part, it operates like a de facto neighborhood association. There are established norms. It requested, and received, a dumpster to help with cleanliness. There are hand-built structures; residents know who the troublemakers are and kick out those with repeated issues.

There is also a level of mistrust toward any kind of officialdom, even well-intentioned individuals wanting to help them get housing. One young woman nearly darted at the sight of this reporter, until she recognized a companion. She said she wants nothing to do with any of “them” because she has active warrants and is afraid that a housing worker would notify law enforcement.

Redgate spoke at length about his neighbors, singling out those that have lived at the site for several years, and the shared confusion and worry over where they will be by winter. He said he had invited a friend to live next to him after that individual was displaced by an encampment clean-up elsewhere in the city. Chapin is, or used to be, a space where the homeless went to be left alone. 

“I got another old man in the back. He’s good people. We’re all good people needing good assistance that weren’t getting it,” he said.

Another resident, Jessica Lane, wishes they all could be left alone. She didn’t say whether she was part of the group applying for housing, but she said that she doesn’t know where to go if the camp is shut down within a couple of weeks.

“Second Light is just not going to work. There’s not enough bed space,” she said, referring to the city’s low-barrier homeless shelter. “Half of us don’t want to go there. I can’t be in a place like that, no offense. My camps are spread out. We’re not that close together. I can’t do an apartment, because I can’t be that closed in.”

Without definitive information from the city, Chapin residents depend on grassroots outreach to fill them in between case manager visits. Many said they want a voice in their fate even more than an open avenue to housing.

“Make them listen. Make them understand,” Redgate said. “There’s some of us out here, you know, we need help. We’re supposed to get housing and all this and that, but nobody’s really paying attention.”

If the camp is closed with residents who still aren’t housed, Lane doesn’t know what the next step would be for her. The city has previously set a goal for 60% of Chapin residents to be housed by the shutdown; the illegal camping ordinance bans homeless people from sleeping on the streets.

“At the end of the day, I don’t know how they can bulldoze. They have nowhere to put us.”
